data.text/markdown: Optimal cut-point value of inverse body-mass index (iBMI) level for predicting diabetes

This notebook shows how to use cutpointpy for estimating the optimal iBMI to predict diabetes mellitus. The data come from the Pima Indians Diabetes Database, available on Kaggle (CC0: Public Domain).

data.text/markdown: Store units here.
Show the data
Use combined strip and plots to show the distribution of the glucose level in the positive and negative class.
Perform optimal cut-point analysis (inverted polarity)

In a previous notebook of this series link_here we discussed the usage of CutpointCalculator and the arguments accepted by the constructor (please see the cited document for details). We shall now invoke the constructor with the default parameters except for the polarity argument. In this case study the polarity is indeed inverted — that is, higher values of iBMI are associated with a lower chance of getting diabetes and vice-versa. Hence we shall set polarity=False to reflect this.
We now proceed as in the other notebook for the optimal cut-point analysis.
As usual we have a look at the returned values, starting with the scalar ones first.
Now the arry-like ones.

data.text/markdown: Let's have a look at the accuracy, sensitivity and specificity yielded by the optimal cut-point.
Show the results graphically
Plot sensitivity and specificity vs. iBMI
Colours and y-axis labels for each metric shown in the chart.

Observe that the shape of the sensitivity/specificity vs. feature value curves is mirrored compared to the ones we got for the glucose level analysis (cutpointboot__glucose_cutoff_for_diabetes.py). This is what we expected, given that the polarity of the problem is inverted here.
Plot ROC curve and show AUC
Check the results with a third-party calculator
For a comparison we can check our results with those generated through MetricGate's Optimal Cutpoint Analysis tool (please find the results here).
